To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) IL‐1R/MyD88 axis is critical for papain‐induce inflammation, 2) MyD88‐signaling is required for the inflammatory response to papains, 3) MyD88 signaling is required in different cell types for the inflammatory response.
IL‐1R‐1–MyD8 signaling in several cell types contributes to the inflammatory response to a single exposure of the airways to the papain allergen.

MyD88‐mediated IL‐1R signaling plays a key role in the early response to a single allergen exposure in the airways and that this response requires several cell types, such as myeloid cells and T cells, but not epithelial cells or ILC2s.

understanding the role of IL‐1 and IL‐33 in the initiation of allergic airway inflammation and the identification of the cell types involved in IL‐1 and/or IL‐33 signaling.

IL‐1R signaling via MyD8 plays a critical role in the early inflammatory response to papains.
the IL‐1R/MyD88 axis is critical for the initiation of the allergic response to papain and that several cell types are involved in MyD8/IL‐1R signaling.
MyD88 is essential for papain‐induction of IL‐1β and IL‐33, and IL‐1β is essential for eosinophil recruitment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IL‐1R–MyD88 signaling pathway is critical for the initiation of inflammation in the lung after a single exposure to the allergen papain.
IL‐1R signaling via MyD8 is required for a first wave of inflammation to a papain challenge.
IL‐1R/MyD88 axis is critical for the initiation of papain‐inducible airway inflammation and that several cell types, including T cells and myeloid cells contribute to this response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IL‐1R/MyD88 axis plays a major role in the initiation of the inflammatory response to papains, and this is a new target for the development of novel therapies for allergic asthma.
